result: The study mapped the developmental origin of 160 interneurons from seven bilateral neuroblast lineages in the Drosophila larval CNS using TEM reconstruction. This represents over a quarter of the ~300 neurons per hemisegment and includes 7,794 presynapses and 19,468 postsynapses.
evaluation: Claims C1, C13, C20, C21, and C104 provide consistent quantitative data about the scope of the study. The mapping of 160 interneurons from 14 neuroblast clones (7 bilateral pairs) is well-documented with specific synapse counts and represents a substantial fraction of the total neurons analyzed.

result: Neuroblast lineages exhibit highly stereotyped and reproducible morphology between left and right hemisegments, including consistent fascicle numbers, cell body positions, and axon/dendrite morphology.
evaluation: Claims C15-C18 demonstrate reproducibility through validation in two hemisegments (A1L and A1R) with similar neuron numbers and morphology. The similarity between genetically marked clones and TEM reconstructions (C16) provides strong validation of the mapping approach.

result: Clonally related neurons from individual neuroblast lineages project widely throughout the neuropil to both sensory and motor domains, lacking shared morphology.
evaluation: Claims C19 and C82 are supported by the broad synaptic distributions shown in Figure 1F-H and contrast with mammalian findings (C81). This wide projection pattern is a key finding that distinguishes Drosophila from mammalian neurogenesis.

result: The neuropil has a functional dorsoventral subdivision where motor processing occurs dorsally and sensory processing occurs ventrally, with premotor neurons targeting the dorsal neuropil and sensory targets projecting ventrally.
evaluation: Claims C22-C25 extend prior work (C22 cites previous studies) with new findings about premotor and postsensory neuron targeting (C23-C24). The data in Figure 2A-C support this functional subdivision along the dorsoventral axis.

result: Most neuroblast lineages generate two morphologically distinct classes of neurons using NBLAST analysis, with each class projecting to either dorsal/motor or ventral/sensory neuropil domains.
evaluation: Claims C26-C30 describe NBLAST clustering results showing two morphological classes per lineage (except NB2-1 and NB3-3). The consistent dorsal/ventral projection pattern for these classes (C28) is well-supported by Figure 2D-J.

result: The two morphological classes identified by NBLAST correspond to NotchON and NotchOFF hemilineages, with NotchON hemilineages projecting to dorsal/motor neuropil and NotchOFF hemilineages projecting to ventral/sensory neuropil.
evaluation: Claims C31-C34 and C42 link morphological classes to hemilineage identity through prior work (C31) and experimental validation using Notch reporters (C34). The hypothesis (C33) is supported by the exception of NB3-3 (C32) and experimental evidence in Figure 3A-B.

result: Notch activity determines dorsal/ventral neuropil projections, as demonstrated by Notchintra misexpression experiments that redirect ventral projections to dorsal neuropil or glia without changing neuron numbers.
evaluation: Claims C35-C37, C39, C41, and C43 describe gain-of-function experiments showing that constitutive Notch expression transforms projection patterns. The quantitative data (C41) showing similar neuron numbers in control vs. Notchintra embryos (p>0.05 for all lineages) supports a transformation rather than cell death mechanism.

result: Each neuroblast coordinately generates sensory and motor processing neurons in parallel through Notch-dependent hemilineage specification, with one half of every GMC division contributing to either sensory or motor networks.
evaluation: Claims C2, C44, and C94 describe the parallel construction of sensory and motor neuropils. This is supported by the finding that each neuroblast generates both NotchON (motor) and NotchOFF (sensory) hemilineages, as demonstrated in the experimental results.

result: Dorsal (NotchON) hemilineages localize both presynapses and postsynapses to the dorsal/motor neuropil and receive input from sensory neurons, while ventral (NotchOFF) hemilineages localize synapses to ventral/sensory neuropil and provide output to motor neurons.
evaluation: Claims C45-C50 describe synapse localization patterns supported by Figure 4A-B. The connectivity diagram (Figure 4B) shows that sensory output goes predominantly to ventral hemilineages and motor input comes from dorsal hemilineages, providing strong support for these claims.

result: Individual hemilineages target their presynapses and postsynapses to distinct, small domains within the sensory or motor neuropil, with neurons in a hemilineage showing greater synaptic position similarity than unrelated neurons.
evaluation: Claims C51-C55 describe the spatial specificity of hemilineage synapse targeting. The data in Figure 4C-G, including quantitative synapse similarity measurements and left-right stereotypy (C53), strongly support these findings.

result: Temporal transcription factors (Hb, Kr, Pdm, Cas) have a radial distribution in the embryonic and larval CNS, with early-born Hb+ neurons positioned deep near the neuropil and late-born Cas+ neurons positioned superficially, allowing radial position to serve as a proxy for temporal identity.
evaluation: Claims C56-C60 confirm prior findings (C56 cites Isshiki et al., 2001) and extend them to the larval stage (C59). Figure 5A-D demonstrates the radial distribution pattern, supporting the use of radial position as a temporal identity proxy.

result: Cortex neurite length (distance from cell body to neuropil entry) can be used as a reproducible proxy for neuronal temporal identity, validated by identifying 54 Hb+ and 44 Cas+ neurons and assigning 70 interneurons to four temporal cohorts.
evaluation: Claims C61-C66 and C97 describe the method for determining temporal identity using cortex neurite length. The reproducibility across hemisegments (C64, Figure 5H) and validation with experimentally identified Hb+ and Cas+ neurons (C61-C62, Figure 5E-G) provide strong support.

result: Temporal identity alone does not confer shared neuronal projections or synapse localization, as neurons with shared temporal identity across different hemilineages show broad projections and no greater synapse similarity than unrelated neurons.
evaluation: Claims C67-C68 are supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 3, which shows that temporal cohorts across hemilineages have broad projections and lack synapse similarity. This negative result is important for understanding that temporal identity requires combination with hemilineage identity.

result: Hemilineage-temporal cohorts target synapses to distinct subdomains within the larger hemilineage domain, with dorsal cohorts preferentially clustering presynapses and ventral cohorts clustering postsynapses, providing finer spatial specificity than hemilineage identity alone.
evaluation: Claims C69-C75 describe how temporal identity subdivides hemilineages into smaller targeting domains. Figure 6A-F provides strong quantitative support showing that hemilineage-temporal cohorts have more similar synaptic positions than hemilineage alone (p<0.05 for presynapses in dorsal and postsynapses in ventral hemilineages).

result: Hemilineage-temporal cohorts share common connectivity with lower network distances than hemilineages alone, with 75% of cohort neurons separated by two synapses or less despite less than 20% being directly connected.
evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C105-C111 describe connectivity patterns supported by Figure 7. The quantitative data showing left-right similarity (C105), network clustering (C106), and specific connectivity distances (C109-C110) provide strong support for shared connectivity within hemilineage-temporal cohorts.

result: Proximity alone cannot explain observed connectivity patterns, as even neurons with high presynapse-postsynapse spatial overlap are not always connected, and hemilineage-temporal cohort connectivity exceeds that predicted by proximity-based models.
evaluation: Claims C5, C112-C115 demonstrate that spatial proximity is insufficient to explain connectivity. Figure 8A-B shows that neurons with high overlap are not always connected and that observed hemilineage-temporal cohort connectivity exceeds proximity-based predictions, supporting an additional layer of specificity.

result: Hemilineage-temporal cohorts have greater shared connectivity than unrelated neurons, temporal cohorts, or hemilineages alone, with temporal identity conferring an added level of connectivity specificity beyond proximity or hemilineage identity.
evaluation: Claims C116-C121 describe enhanced connectivity within hemilineage-temporal cohorts. Figure 8C-E provides quantitative support showing greater shared connectivity for presynapses (C116, p<0.0001) and differential effects for postsynapses (C117), supporting the combinatorial model (C121).

result: The proprioceptive circuit (Jaam-Eve-Saaghi) is assembled from three distinct hemilineage-temporal cohorts: late-born NB5-2 ventral (Jaam), late-born NB3-3 (Eve+), and late-born NB5-2 dorsal (Saaghi), supporting a model where hemilineage-temporal cohorts are units of connectivity for motor circuit assembly.
evaluation: Claims C76-C80, C92-C93, and C103 describe the developmental origin of a functionally characterized circuit. Figure 9 shows that all three components are late-born neurons from specific hemilineage-temporal cohorts, with Jaam in NotchOFF (sensory processing) and Saaghi in NotchON (motor processing) hemilineages, consistent with their functional roles.

result: Neuroblast lineage, hemilineage, and temporal identity act sequentially to progressively refine neuronal projections, synapse localization, and connectivity, with lineages having broad projections, hemilineages restricting to motor/sensory domains, and temporal identity providing subdomain specificity.
evaluation: Claims C14 and C102 summarize the hierarchical organization demonstrated throughout the study. The sequential refinement from broad lineage projections (C19) to hemilineage domains (C55) to hemilineage-temporal subdomains (C74) is well-supported by the cumulative evidence.

result: NotchOFF hemilineages generate ascending and descending projection neurons and produce more complex and lengthy neurons than NotchON hemilineages, similar to patterns observed in larval brain lineages.
evaluation: Claims C38 and C40 describe morphological differences between hemilineages. Figure 3—figure supplement 1 shows that ventral (NotchOFF) hemilineages have significantly longer axons (p=0.0034), and C40 cites similar findings in larval brain lineages (Lee et al., 2020), suggesting a conserved mechanism.

result: Neuroblast spatial identity determines lineage-specific projection patterns, and neurons within a hemilineage likely respond similarly to global pathfinding cues while different hemilineages express different palettes of guidance receptors.
evaluation: Claims C83, C87, and C88 propose mechanisms for how developmental identity translates to projection patterns. While the stereotyped projections (C83) support the first part, the proposed mechanisms about guidance receptor expression (C87-C88) are speculative inferences without direct experimental evidence of receptor expression or response to guidance cues.

result: Neuropil guidance cue gradients exist along multiple axes, and vertebrate V2 progenitors may generate hemilineages through Notch signaling, with molecular subclasses potentially arising from temporal patterning.
evaluation: Claims C86, C89, and C90 cite prior work on guidance cues and vertebrate neurogenesis. C86 references established gradients, C89 cites evidence for vertebrate hemilineages, and C90 proposes a testable hypothesis about temporal patterning in vertebrates based on the Drosophila findings.

result: The parallel generation of sensory and motor neurons may maintain sensory/motor balance during evolution, and temporal identity likely acts combinatorially with hemilineage identity to direct precise targeting, with implications for experimental design.
evaluation: Claims C95, C96, C99, and C100 are speculative proposals about evolutionary implications (C95), methodological considerations (C96), and mechanistic models (C99-C100). While these are reasonable inferences from the data, they lack direct experimental support and represent hypotheses for future testing.

result: The three-dimensional location of each hemilineage-temporal cohort synaptic cluster is identical on left and right sides of A1, ruling out stochastic self-avoidance as a mechanism.
evaluation: Claim C98 states that data exists showing left-right stereotypy of synaptic clusters but notes it is not shown ('data not shown'). While this is consistent with other left-right stereotypy findings (C53, C64), the absence of presented data makes this claim uncertain despite being plausible.

result: Lineage information, hemilineage identity, and temporal identity can be accurately predicted using morphological features such as fascicle number and radial position.
evaluation: Claim C101 summarizes the methodological advances demonstrated throughout the study. The successful use of fascicle number for lineage identification (C15-C16) and cortex neurite length for temporal identity (C62-C66) with validation through multiple approaches supports this methodological result.

result: Three developmental mechanisms generate neuronal diversity in Drosophila: spatial patterning establishing neuroblast identity, temporal transcription factor cascades (Hb, Kr, Pdm, Cas) specifying GMC identity, and Notch-dependent hemilineage formation through asymmetric division.
evaluation: Claims C6-C12 summarize established knowledge about Drosophila neurogenesis from prior work (citing Skeath and Thor, 2003; Isshiki et al., 2001). These background claims provide the foundation for the current study and are well-supported by the cited literature.

result: Prior work shows that mammalian clonal neurons have similar location, morphology, and connectivity, and that Drosophila larval hemilineages have different projection patterns and can elicit different behaviors when activated.
evaluation: Claims C81, C84, C85, and C91 cite prior work on mammalian neurogenesis (C81) and Drosophila hemilineages (C84, C85, C91). These background claims are appropriately cited and provide context for comparing the current findings to previous studies.
